column11: Berakhot 33b: ‘The Gemara responds: Indeed, for Moses fear of Heaven is a minor matter. As Rabbi Ḥanina stated: It is comparable to one who is asked for a large vessel and he has one, it seems to him like a small vessel because he owns it. However, one who is asked for just a small vessel and he does not have one, it seems to him like a large vessel. Therefore, Moses could say: What does the Lord your God ask of you other than to fear, because in his eyes it was a minor matter.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 33b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and this is what they stated in Berachos (33b): "Fear of Heaven relative to Moshe is a minor thing"; for relative to Knesset Israel the Blessed Name asks of them merely this awe (Devarim 10:12),...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: [So here,] Scripture spoke in her praise, not her disgrace, for her eyes’ being “tender” was on account of the deeds of Esav being hateful in her eyes — and it is known that anger and desire are two opposites. column15: And in this world, man attains merely a glimmer from the deep reserves of light that the Blessed Name is destined to reveal in the future; just as the Targum renders “A Song of Ascents” (Psalms 120:1): “to bring up the waters of the deep,” which means that the subterranean deep ascends to moisten and vitalize the world, as stated in the Gemara (Sukkah 53a): “The higher it rises, the more the earth is saturated.”

column11: Deuteronomy 10:12: ‘And now, O Israel, what does the ETERNAL your God demand of you? column15: And Israel illuminates this very darkness. column11: Zohar, Beshalach 25:339-26:348: ‘Then HE (Moses) CRIED UNTO THE LORD, AND THE LORD SHOWED HIM A TREE, without deviating right or left. This is symbolized by the sound of the Shophar, which is thrust forth in a straight line from a narrow opening and breaks through the firmaments in order to stir up the Spirit above. It is true, we are told, that “Isaac did meditate in the field” (Gen. 24, 63); but there are special reasons for this; and besides, the field where he prayed was not an ordinary field. WHICH, WHEN HE CAST IT INTO THE WATERS, THE WATERS WERE MADE SWEET. The tree is a symbol of the Torah, which is “a tree of life to those who lay hold upon her” (Prov. 3, 18), and the Torah and the Holy One, blessed be He, are one.’ R. Abba said: ‘The “Tree” is a direct symbol of the Holy One, for it says: “The tree of the field is (the supernal) Adam” (Deut. 20, 19).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Beshalach 25:339-26:348) to illuminate his exposition here (“as is known, awe is the gate to enter into faith (Zohar II, 60a); and its primary seat is in the heart as written in Yoma (72b) on the verse "seeing he has no heart" (Mishlei 17:16); and as...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Yoma 72b: ‘Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yonatan said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, as he has no heart?” (Proverbs 17:16)? This expresses the following sentiment: Woe to them, haters of Torah scholars, a euphemism for the Torah scholars themselves, who immerse themselves in Torah and have no fear of Heaven. They are fools; they try to acquire the wisdom of Torah, but since they have no fear of Heaven in their hearts they lack the ability to do so.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and its primary seat is in the heart as written in Yoma (72b) on the verse "seeing he has no heart" (Mishlei 17:16); and as written in Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b): "the Merciful One desires the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: The giving of the Torah aiming to absorb it within the heart: "write them upon the table of your heart," and "upon their heart will I write it"; for "the Merciful One desires the heart" (Sanhedrin 106b); and whoever possesses awe of Heaven has all Torah and wisdom implanted in his heart (Devarim Rabbah, Berachah), awe being centered in the heart (Yoma 72b); termed "the Torah of Moses," for whom awe was a simple matter (Berakhot 33b), embodying Da'at which binds Chochmah and Binah.
column15: And this is what the Zohar notes (Naso 135b): regarding the eighth king, Hadar, death is no longer mentioned, because concerning him it is recorded: “and his wife's name was Mehetabel”—meaning he had acquired holy awe; for a woman alludes to the fear of Hashem, as it is written (Proverbs 31:30): “a woman that fears the Lord.”

column11: Proverbs 17:16: ‘What good is money in the hand of a foolTo purchase wisdom, when that person has no mind?’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Proverbs 17:16) to illuminate his exposition here (“and its primary seat is in the heart as written in Yoma (72b) on the verse "seeing he has no heart" (Mishlei 17:16); and as written in Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b): "the Merciful One desires the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: It is taught in the Holy Zohar (Toldot 145a): “‘She opens her mouth with wisdom’—this is the Beit of Bereishit; ‘and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue’ (Proverbs 31:26)—this is Abraham, through whom He created the world and concerning whom He speaks continuously.

column11: Sanhedrin 106b: ‘And Rabbi Yitzḥak says: What is the meaning of that which is written: “But to the wicked, God says: What have you to do to declare My statutes, and that you have taken My covenant in your mouth” (Psalms 50:16)? The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Doeg the wicked: Why do you speak of My statutes and My Torah? When you reach the Torah portion of murderers and the Torah portion of slanderers, how do you teach them? You have violated both. With regard to the end of that verse: “And that you have taken My covenant in your mouth” (Psalms 50:16), Rabbi Ami says: Doeg’s Torah is only insincere lip service, as it is in his mouth but not in his heart. He does not have a profound understanding of the Torah and does not commit himself to the performance of its mitzvot.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 106b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as written in Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b): "the Merciful One desires the heart"; unlike lip service, where it is required that the mouth be cleaved unto the heart; and this is the entire...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Isaiah 6:10: ‘Dull that people’s mind,Stop its ears,And seal its eyes—Lest, seeing with its eyesAnd hearing with its ears,It also grasp with its mind,And repent and save itself.”’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Isaiah 6:10) to illuminate his exposition here (“when they merit the complete purification of the heart, wherein "his heart shall understand, and he shall return, and be healed" (Yeshayah 6:10).”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: Its only rectification being Torah study, which likewise derives from Chochmah, as I wrote elsewhere. Gevurah stemming from Binah ("anger from your heart"), being constructive only in a scholar when tempered by Chochmah from the right chamber, the left remaining foolish. And at the right is the wise heart, lust dwelling in the heart containing vital good, preserving the species and procreating souls.
column15: Meaning supernal worlds are compounded of two rungs: male and female, receiving force and bestowing force, lights and vessels. As in Isaiah 6:3: “And one called unto another,” rendered: “and they receive one from another,” each receiving from above and bestowing below.

column11: Shemot Rabbah 2:6: ‘“Moses said: I will turn now, and see this great sight; why will the bush not burn?” (Exodus 3:3). “Moses said: I will turn [asura] now and see.” Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Moses took five steps at that moment, as it is stated: “I will turn [asura]. The numerical value of the additional heh alludes to the five steps that Moses took. now and see.” Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: He turned around and looked, as it is stated: “The Lord saw that he had turned to see” (Exodus 3:4). Once he looked at it, the Holy One blessed be He said: ‘He is suitable to shepherd Israel.’ “The Lord saw that he turned to see, and God called to him from the midst of the bush and He said: ‘Moses, Moses.’ He said: ‘Here I am’” (Exodus 3:4).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shemot Rabbah 2:6) to illuminate his exposition here (“And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, merited this insight immediately at the first revelation at the bush, saying: "Here am I"—ready for the Priesthood, "Here am I"—ready for the Monarchy...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: “Noah was a righteous man.” In Tanchuma (Nitzavim 1): This is what Scripture says (Proverbs 12:7): “The wicked are overthrown, and are not; but the house of the righteous shall stand” — whenever the Holy One scrutinizes the deeds of the wicked and overturns them, they have no remedy; He overturned the deeds of the Flood generation and they had no survival, as said: “and He blotted out all existence”.

column11: Zohar, Toldot 14:108-15:119: ‘The “field” again is the “field which the Lord hath blessed” (Gen. 27, 27). When a man has penetrated into the mystery of Wisdom and perfected himself therein, then Solomon tells him to “build his house” (Prov. 24, 27), i.e. to cultivate his soul in his body, so as to attain perfection. Hence, when Isaac digged and prepared the well in peace he called it Rehoboth (wide places), and all was done in the right manner. Happy the righteous by whose works the Holy One sustains the world, as it says: “For the upright shall inhabit the land” (Prov. 2, 21), where the term yishkenu (they will inhabit) may be read yashkinu (they shall cause to be inhabited).’’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Toldot 14:108-15:119) to illuminate his exposition here (“and "the lip of truth shall be established forever" (Mishlei 12:19), the Zohar expounding (I, 141b): "it is not written 'was established' in the past, but 'shall be established' in the future";...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Shabbat 10a: ‘Speaking of prayer, the Gemara relates that Rava saw Rav Hamnuna, who was prolonging his prayer. He said about him: They abandon eternal life, the study of Torah, and engage in temporal life, prayer, which includes requests for mundane needs. The Gemara explains: And Rav Hamnuna held that the time for prayer is distinct and the time for Torah is distinct. The time that one devotes to prayer is not at the expense of the time devoted to Torah study. Similarly, the Gemara relates that Rabbi Yirmeya was sitting before Rabbi Zeira and they were engaged in the study of halakha. The time for prayer was approaching and it was getting late and Rabbi Yirmeya was hurrying to conclude the subject that they were studying in order to pray.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 10a) to illuminate his exposition here (“for the entire life of this world is termed "temporary life" (Shabbat 10a); and after being refined and whitened across all the exiles through repentance (Daniel 12:10), they will return to those...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: But in truth, on the contrary, it [Torah] gives him eternal life, as they said [Shabbos 10a], and also temporal life, as they said [Shabbos 30b] regarding David, and in Bava Metzia [86a] regarding Rabbah bar Nachmani [whom the Angel of Death could not take while he was engaged in Torah]. And the evil inclination is the Angel of Death, as they said [Bava Basra 16a]; and just as [Torah] saves from the evil inclination, so it saves from the Angel of Death — as at the Giving of the Torah, when they were “free of the evil inclination” and of the Angel of Death.
column15: Then it is called the “light of Torah,” as the Talmud states (Shabbat 10a): that prayer is life of the hour, while Torah is eternal life. And for one upon whom Hashem seals His Name as refined in his inward heart, his prayer likewise becomes eternal life.

column11: Shabbat 151b: ‘It was also taught in a baraita with regard to the appreciation of life: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: Perform mitzvot while you still find opportunities, and you have the financial means, and you are still under your own control. column13: And this is the root of evil within biological birth, completely independent of human deed; matching Chagigah (15a), Sotah (22a), and Bava Batra (16a): "You created the righteous, You created the wicked"; having created the yetzer hara from the dawn of Creation, formed alongside man at his very conception; as it is said: "for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Bereishis 8:21)—expounded: "from the moment he shakes free from his mother's womb" (Sanhedrin 91b).

column11: Kohelet Rabbah 7:1: ‘“A good name is better than fine oil, and the day of death than the day of one's birth” (Ecclesiastes 7:1).“A good name is better than fine oil.” Fine oil descends, a good name ascends. Fine oil is temporary, a good name is eternal. Fine oil is finite, a good name is infinite. Fine oil costs money, a good name is free. Fine oil is for the living, a good name is for the living and for the dead. Fine oil is for the wealthy, a good name is for the poor and the wealthy. Fine oil wafts from the inner chamber to the banquet hall, a good name carries from one end of the world to the other end. Fine oil falls on a corpse and putrefies, as it is stated: “Flies of death putrefy and ferment blended oil” (Ecclesiastes 10:1).…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Kohelet Rabbah 7:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“for precious oil emits its fragrance merely from the chamber to the parlor (Koheles Rabbah 7:1); for the wholly righteous man operates within measured boundaries, each according to his measured...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And these correspond to the three names that Koheles Rabbah (7:1) states every person possesses: one that he calls himself—through his own striving; and one given by others—from his parents; and one inscribed in the book of his generation—from his divine soul-root: "For Hashem's portion is His people" (Devarim 32:9).
column15: “From pursuing your affairs on My holy day”—for human desires and actions, even good and noble deeds, are exceptionally finite, enduring merely for the moment. Therefore they are forbidden on Shabbat, for Shabbat is named “My holy day”—signifying that the Blessed Name is engaged then in bestowing eternal, everlasting spiritual bounty.

column11: Avodah Zarah 17a: ‘Elazar ben Durdayya said: Clearly the matter depends on nothing other than myself. He placed his head between his knees and cried loudly until his soul left his body. column11: Yevamot 16a: ‘Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas recited this verse about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: “I have been young, and now am old; yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread” (Psalms 37:25). column11: Sanhedrin 37a: ‘Reish Lakish says that the source to rely on them not to transgress is from here: “Your temples [rakkatekh] are like a pomegranate split open” (Song of Songs 6:7), which teaches that even the empty people [reikanin] among you are as full of mitzvot as the pomegranate is full of seeds. Rabbi Zeira says that the source is from here: The verse states concerning the occasion when Isaac blessed Jacob: “And he smelled the smell of his garments, and blessed him, and said: See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). column11: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan interpreted the verse regarding Abraham our patriarch. When the Holy One blessed be He said to him: “Go you from your land, from your birthplace” (Genesis 12:1), to what was it analogous? To a flask of balsam oil that was placed in one corner and its fragrance did not diffuse. One came and moved it from its place and its fragrance diffused. So, too, the Holy One blessed be He said to Abraham: ‘Abraham, you have many good deeds, you have many mitzvot, move yourself around in the world and your name will be exalted in the world.’ “Go, you,” what is written thereafter? “I will render you a great nation” (Genesis 12:2).“Therefore, young women love you.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“and like Daniel, Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah, who are the possessors of the good name mentioned in the Midrash (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3) on the verse "A good name is better than precious...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column15: Now behold, here it is stated: “And God said, Let there be light”; and when the Blessed Name said “Let there be,” the light surely came into being—why then does it add “and there was light”? column11: Sanhedrin 104a: ‘The Gemara continues and asks: For what reason did the tanna’im not enumerate the wicked Amon among the kings with no share in the World-to-Come? The Gemara answers: He is not enumerated due to the honor of Josiah, his righteous son. The Gemara challenges: Let us also not enumerate Manasseh due to the honor of Hezekiah, his righteous father. The Gemara explains: The son confers merit upon the father, as it is to the father’s credit that he raised a righteous son; but the father does not confer merit upon the son, as it is written: “None delivers from My hand” (Deuteronomy 32:39). Abraham does not deliver his son Ishmael from the judgment of Heaven; Isaac does not deliver his son Esau from judgment.…’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 104a) to illuminate his exposition here (“for if a person is not righteous, he can be redeemed through his seed, for "a son confers merit upon his father," as written in Sanhedrin (104a); and "the remnant of Joseph" refers to his...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And this is a principle operating within every person; only that whoever fails to examine the chambers of his heart every moment does not stand cognizant of this at all, it occurring outside his conscious awareness. column11: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 2: ‘These are the generations of Noah (Gen. 6:9). R. Tanhuma the son of Abba began the discussion of this subject with the verse: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that is wise winneth souls (Prov. 11:30). R. column11: Shabbat 77b: ‘On the topic of the nature of the world, the Gemara relates that Rabbi Zeira found Rav Yehuda, who was standing at the entrance of his father-in-law’s house, and observed that he was in an especially cheerful mood. He therefore posed questions to him on a variety of topics unrelated to halakha. He asked: Why do goats walk in front of the flock and then ewes follow? He said to him: It is just as it was in the creation of the world, which at first was dark and then light followed. column11: Bereshit Rabbah 2:5: ‘Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Ḥiyya the Great, Rabbi Abahu said: Right from the beginning of the creation of the world, the Holy One blessed be He foresaw the actions of the righteous and the actions of the wicked. column11: Chagigah 15a: ‘Aḥer said to him: Rabbi Akiva, your teacher, did not say so, but explained the verse as follows: Everything has its opposite: He created the righteous, He created the wicked; He created the Garden of Eden, He created Gehenna. column15: “And the earth was unformed (tohu) and void (bohu).” It is stated (in Sefer HaBahir, §2): “Tohu is something that confounds/misleads human beings; Bohu means ‘it is in it’ (bo hu).” The meaning of this is: when Hashem shows a person that He validates and grants space to his divine service, the person must then serve Hashem with even greater humility and must not assume personal pride or assertiveness simply because Hashem revealed that his toil holds significance.

column11: Bava Batra 16a: ‘The Gemara continues to discuss Job’s statements: “Although You know that I am not wicked, and there is none that can deliver out of Your hand” (Job 10:7). Rava says: Job sought to exempt the whole world from judgment, claiming that all of a person’s actions are directed by God, and therefore one cannot be held culpable for his misdeeds. Job said before God: Master of the Universe, You created the ox with split hooves, making it kosher, and You created the donkey with closed hooves, making it forbidden; You created the Garden of Eden, and You created Gehenna; and similarly, You created righteous people and You created wicked people; who can restrain You? Seeing that You created people as either righteous or wicked, You cannot later complain about their actions.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 16a) to illuminate his exposition here (“And regarding this they stated in Chagigah (15a), Sotah (22a), and Bava Batra (16a): "You have created the righteous, You have created the wicked"; yet behold, they explicitly declared (Niddah...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.

column11: Niddah 16b: ‘The Gemara notes: But this angel does not say: Will he be wicked or righteous? People have free will to serve God or not, as it is stated: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you other than to fear the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 10:12). The fact that God asks of the Jewish people to fear Him indicates that it is a person’s choice to do so.’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Niddah 16b) to illuminate his exposition here (“yet behold, they explicitly declared (Niddah 16b): "whether one will be righteous or wicked the angel does not decree"! column13: Yet it is equally true that free will is granted and choice rests in man's hand, for "whether one will be righteous or wicked the angel does not declare" [Niddah 16b], otherwise Torah has no validity, which is a foundational axiom as Maimonides writes in Hilchot Teshuvah; how this reconciles with ultimate Unity is exceedingly profound, and all the philosophical efforts of scholars to resolve Divine foreknowledge and human free will fail to satisfy those who perceive true Unity—that there is literally none else.

column11: Berakhot 48a: ‘The Gemara relates that Abaye and Rava, when they were children, were seated before Rabba. Rabba said to them: To whom does one recite blessings? column11: Sukkah 52a: ‘Abaye said: In that situation, if instead of that man it had been one whom I hate, a euphemism for himself, he would not have been able to restrain himself from sinning. column11: Rosh Hashanah 2a: ‘On the first of Shevat is the New Year for the tree; the fruit of a tree that was formed prior to that date belong to the previous tithe year and cannot be tithed together with fruit that was formed after that date; this ruling is in accordance with the statement of Beit Shammai. column11: Bereshit Rabbah 13:13: ‘How much rain needs to fall to constitute “permeation”? column11: Yoma 69b: ‘Zechariah the prophet said to them: See and understand that if you kill this evil inclination the world will be destroyed because as a result there will also no longer be any desire to procreate. column11: Sukkah 52b: ‘The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: If this scoundrel, the evil inclination, accosted you, seeking to tempt you to sin, drag it to the study hall and study Torah. column11: Vayikra Rabbah 24:6: ‘Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazi said: Why was the portion of forbidden sexual relations juxtaposed to the portion of “[you shall be] holy”? column13: And one must also examine one who cohabits with a gentile woman (bo'el aramis), regarding whom they stated there that Avraham does not draw him up (Eruvin 19a), where according to their words he too is excluded from these protected sinners of Israel; and in Tosafos [Bava Metzia 58b] they asked why he was not enumerated there, answering that one does not descend on account of this transgression alone without another sin, see there; from the golden altar, and in the last chapter of Chagigah (27a) [where] he made a kal va-chomer from the salamander — except three who do not ascend immediately; but some of them are judged forever, such as [the heretics], and…

column15: Wherefore, after Avraham our Father circumcised himself and clarified his attributes, then Sodom and her daughter cities were overturned; for when a soul from Israel is refined in any character trait, the nation opposing that trait is automatically nullified; wherefore when Abraham removed from himself the foreskin of his flesh, the foreskin of the entire world was abolished—namely Sodom and her daughters.

column11: Yevamot 72a: ‘The Gemara suggests: Let us say that this amoraic dispute as to whether or not one who had been circumcised but his residual foreskin was drawn forward is considered uncircumcised by Torah law is parallel to the following dispute between tanna’im. As it is taught in the Tosefta (Shabbat 16:7): One whose foreskin was drawn forward, and similarly, one who was born circumcised, and a convert who converted when he was already circumcised, and a child whose appropriate time for circumcision already passed and he was still uncircumcised, and all others who require circumcision, which, as the Gemara parenthetically adds, comes to include one who has two foreskins, both of which must be removed, may be circumcised only during the day. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon says: If the circumcision is performed at its appropriate time, i.e., on the eighth day,’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 72a) to illuminate his exposition here (“yet one whose foreskin is drawn down remains biblically circumcised, requiring rabbinic re-circumcision merely for outward appearance (Yevamos 72a); and this is what the Talmud means by "Avraham...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And from Abaye and Rava onward is after the midday point of the Talmud, and then began the total gloom and darkness that followed the Talmudic era, than which there is no greater darkness, for everything divides into three phases, and the night comprises three watches: they are Tannaim, Amoraim, and all the subsequent post-Talmudic generations; and from Abaye and Rava onward corresponds to after midnight, and precisely then is a time of far greater divine favor, as stated in Yevamot (72a) and in the Zohar.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:38
column15: And this is the distinction between one born in the house and one bought with money: one born in the house is circumcised on the eighth day, while one bought with money is circumcised on day one, and akin to what is taught in the Talmud (Shabbat 135a): anyone whose mother is ritually impure with childbirth is circumcised on the eighth day.

column11: I Samuel 16:7: ‘But GOD said to Samuel, “Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature, for I have rejected him. For [GOD sees] not as humans see; humans see only what is visible, but GOD sees into the heart.”’ Context and connection to Machshavot Charutz: In Machshavot Charutz 8, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (I Samuel 16:7) to illuminate his exposition here (“and none rescues him except the Blessed Name Himself, Who "looks on the heart" (I Shmuel 16:7), seeing that in the ultimate depths of his heart he too remains circumcised! And Pinchas—who is...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the supernal levels of Thought (Machshavah), the rectification of human desire and intellect, and the inner light of the Oral Torah developed in Machshavot Charutz.
column13: And concerning the priests Scripture states: "unto Me" (Li), which denotes an enduring covenant for all eternity, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Vayikra Rabbah 2:2); and even regarding the cohen of the lowliest spiritual stature, so long as he descends from Aaron's seed, even though not a trace of holiness appears visible upon him— "for man looks on the outward appearance, but Hashem looks on the heart" (I Samuel 16:7), and He has already promised: "If you can break My covenant of the day and My covenant of the night, etc." (Jeremiah 33:20–21) concerning the eternal covenant of the priesthood.
column15: Therefore, before man in this physical world this hidden fortitude buried in the deep remains concealed, and on account of this concealment man experiences trembling awe, as it is written (Hosea 3:5): “And they shall fear the Lord and His goodness,” meaning that the Jew trembles in his heart, pondering: “Who knows what is prepared for me in the depths and what awaits me there?”—showing that from this concealed deep emerge all facets of sacred awe.
